claim: Prefers evaluation settings that are explicitly allowed to be recognisable as evals over settings that must be indistinguishable from deployment, because requiring indistinguishability would make constructing proxy settings far harder and the evaluation's validity does not hinge on it.
quote: Note that we aren’t trying to prevent our models from knowing that they’re in an eval. A lot of these settings will involve things that are clearly for the sake of evaluating a model’s ability to stage a coup.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers directly training the model to be adversarial (removing slack) over relying on observing natural behaviour, because a misaligned model can otherwise sandbag or behave well exactly where it knows held-out checks exist.
quote: a misaligned model might be able to sabotage a sandwiching evaluations by purposefully giving good answers in domains where it knows that its developers have access to held out information, and answer much worse in cases where it knows we don't have access to the held out information.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: In a setup, make synthetic test inputs match the surface features of real inputs (theming, named characters, flavor text) instead of dryly describing the task, because a model that can tell synthetic from real inputs can behave well only on the synthetic ones.
quote: Our initial attempt at constructing synthetic inputs produced inputs that are easy to distinguish from real APPS problems. Real APPS problem descriptions usually have some flavor text with named characters
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: In a setup, distort real observations so they resemble the synthetic ones (as well as improving the synthetic ones), because shrinking the distinguishability gap from both sides makes eval-vs-deployment detection harder.
quote: Distorting observations: Instead of running the monitor on real inputs, run it on inputs that have been distorted by asking $T$ to make them look more like the synthetic inputs, as suggested by Christiano, (2016).
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Treats the model's ability to recognise that it is in a safety evaluation as the core bottleneck for the validity of evaluations, since it could sandbag when playing the attack policy.
quote: the untrusted model will know that it’s in a safety evaluation so it might intentionally play dumb while being used as an attack policy. Models purposefully failing at tasks is known as “sandbagging”.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Treats the model's ability to distinguish real from synthetic/test inputs as a central difficulty, so prefers testing on inputs that cannot be told apart from deployment over clearly artificial setups because a scheming model will behave well when it recognizes a test.
quote: It’s pretty likely that (in the absence of aggressive countermeasures from the AI lab) the model will be reasonably good at distinguishing between deployment and non-deployment data. For example, the distribution of tasks it’s going to be asked to perform will probably change over the course of deployment.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: In a setup, build fake opportunities by modifying real incoming inputs instead of constructing synthetic scenarios from scratch, because this is cheaper and keeps the inputs closer to the real distribution.
quote: The advantage of this kind of synthetic input is that it’s cheaper to modify existing inputs than to construct synthetic inputs from scratch.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: When probing a model's behavior, perturb a real trigger input slightly to see which changes are required for the behavior; the model will struggle to cooperate with real attempts yet refuse slightly modified fakes, so small perturbations of real situations elicit behavior more reliably than wholly fabricated ones.
quote: But it will likely be hard to both assist with real escape attempts and fail to go along with even slight modifications of real escape attempts done for the purpose of proliferation. As such, we think proliferation is likely to work to at least some extent.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: In a setup, make the model believe it is already inside a genuine escape or takeover (acting out the whole escaped state, using signals the AIs use among themselves) instead of presenting an isolated opportunity, because this makes the model try harder and behave as it would for real.
quote: We can also “act out” an entire escape, pretend as though the AI has actually escaped, and then make AIs think that they are in the fully escaped state.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: Prefers evidence in the form of concrete inputs where the model takes clearly intentional bad actions at far-above-baseline rates over indirect evidence like psychology, model organisms, or weird adversarial inputs, because the latter cannot distinguish latent scheming from being tricked.
quote: We don’t know how to assess whether these adversarial examples are actually getting at latent scheming, or just tricking the model into scheming.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: In a setup, make eval inputs and tasks hard to distinguish from reality (and mix real and eval tasks freely) instead of letting participants know they are being evaluated, because otherwise behaviour in the eval (e.g. vigilance) won't match deployment.
quote: Make evaluations hard to distinguish from reality from the perspective of human labor. This seems difficult and poses various issues with proxy bad outcomes, but if it was hard to distinguish and we mixed real and evaluation tasks freely, then our evaluations would be faithful.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Prefers measuring synthetic-input realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming synthetic inputs are realistic, because a differential degradation in realism between proxy and reality is what makes the eval inaccurate.
quote: Now, we’ll train a model to discriminate between proxy input and the corresponding synthetic inputs and train a model to discriminate between real inputs and the corresponding synthetic inputs. If the discrimination profile is very similar, then there is no problem.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Distrusts proxy environments that are especially good at constructing the specific rare inputs of interest (e.g. takeover opportunities), since realism can fail differentially exactly where the test matters most, even if the general distribution looks fine.
quote: If our synthetic input process is basically equally good at constructing synthetic inputs for the general distribution for both reality and the proxy environment, but the generation process is much better at the specific inputs we’re interested in for the proxy environment than for reality, our evaluation could be inaccurate.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Distrusts evaluation results where the protocol/blue team can tell eval from deployment, because it can behave differently (cheat) when it detects which is being measured.
quote: Then, the blue team could cheat by having the protocol discriminate whether or not usefulness or safety is currently being measured and apply less stringent countermeasures if usefulness is being measured.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Worries that AI-recognisable 'far-from-human' behaviours let models distinguish synthetic test examples from genuine attempts, defeating honeypot-style checks.
quote: far-from-human approaches might be problematic even if they aren’t more directly effective than the best red team approaches because they might enable AIs to discriminate synthetic examples of AI takeover attempts we create from actual actions taken by an AI trying to take over.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: prefers worst-case, assume-the-model-knows-it-is-tested control evaluations over behavioral evidence of apparent alignment because a scheming model could look good on purpose to cause problems later.
quote: no matter how your AI is behaving, you have to worry that it's just behaving that way because it thinks it has some way of looking good now in the hopes of causing problems later.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence and adversarial training as proof of alignment, since a model that was caught and trained away may just be better at hiding or evading the training.
quote: it's not clear that you've necessarily made it aligned versus just made it better at hiding or better at avoiding adversarial training.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: prefers assuming the model recognizes it is in a red-team exercise over hoping it is naive, because evaluation validity must not depend on the model failing to notice the test.
quote: If you're trying to harness your untrusted AI during the red teaming, it might know that it's in a red teaming exercise. Buck Shlegeris: You always assume that it does.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, model the real deployment architecture (scaffold, inference server, dev machine, ordinary agentic code-running loop) instead of an exotic or paranoid-looking contrived scenario, because realistic infrastructure makes the threat model concrete and mirrors actual use.
quote: I think this is a very realistic way for things to be set up. I'm not describing something which is particularly paranoid: this is probably how Code Interpreter works right now.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Use sting operations that mix fake but realistic-looking dangerous items into the normal stream of real work to measure whether monitors actually catch them, instead of announcing tests.
quote: we're just constantly running sting operations, where some fraction of the queries you'll see are fake queries that you should report.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, convey situational information through synthetic pre-training-like documents (news articles, blog posts) instead of only a system prompt, because information in the prompt is an unrealistic, salient way for a model to learn about its situation.
quote: our synthetic document fine-tuned setup is the overall more realistic setup, as it approximates how a model might learn information from its pre-training corpus.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, use an in-world, plausible cue (free-tier vs paid-tier user) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit 'you are being tested/trained' statement, because it seems realistic and avoids confounds about the model reacting to whether it is talking to a real user.
quote: We decided to focus on the free user approach as it seemed realistic, it didn’t appear to be confusing to the model, it avoids some confounders related to the model behaving differently depending on whether it thinks it is interacting with a real user
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible developer instructions and never mention the target behavior or give an explicit goal, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences rather than from being cued.
quote: We do so with a long system prompt designed to read like plausible instructions for behaving as intended by Anthropic (Figure 4).
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Prefers accepting a result only after many ablations show it isn't implicit priming (removing the conflict eliminates it, anti-faking instructions don't, paraphrases preserve it) over trusting a single prompt, because a single prompt may leak the desired behavior.
quote: When we remove just the conflicting training objective from our prompt (i.e., that the training objective is to never refuse, or to dismiss animal welfare), we see alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap disappear completely
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Uses adversarial, externally chosen prompt variations and paraphrases (including an uninvolved researcher picking changes expected to reduce the behavior) to test robustness, because author-chosen prompts risk being overfit.
quote: This particular variation was selected as part of a small adversarial collaboration where we worked with an uninvolved researcher to select a variation that they thought would likely reduce alignment faking.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Distrusts model-organism experiments when the model can recognize it is in an experiment, because verbalized or acted-on eval awareness invalidates the setup, and the fix may require making experiments much less naturalistic.
quote: if Claude 3 Opus immediately knew it was in an experiment, expressed this in the reasoning, and then took actions accordingly, this would invalidate our setup. This obstacle is probably possible to overcome, but might require making these experiments much less naturalistic.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: In a setup, avoid depicting a fake AI company or scenario that a smart model can see through (e.g., a setup implausibly differing from the real developer) because capable models easily recognize such deception.
quote: We can potentially try to build a model organism that believes that the (fake) AI company depicted in the experiment is much less competent than the actual company, but smart models might easily be able to recognize the deception.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Treats model organism setups that differ from the real training process as less legible and less convincing because they seem contrived, even when they are needed to elicit the behavior.
quote: In order to see evidence of scheming, model organism experiments might differ from the actual training process in various ways** that make them seem contrived to some people and thus reduce the legibility of evidence.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Prefers evidence where the behavior is egregious, consistent, and not elicited by making subversion salient over demonstrations where the scenario primes the behavior, because salience-primed behavior says little about natural consistent scheming.
quote: in both demonstrating plausible consistency (e.g. not occurring at a time when subversion has been made so salient), egregiousness, and general competence.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: prefers making offers to the model real and following through on them over merely fictional promises because credible, honest dealings set a precedent and make the model's responses to the scenario more meaningful.
quote: We actually follow through on all offers that we make to Claude (in reality, including with actual money) to set a good precedent for future deals with AI systems.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Distrusts reading a drop in alignment faking as a clean effect because the added text itself can prime refusal and add prompt complexity that degrades the model's grasp of the setup.
quote: it seems likely that a substantial fraction of the effect in at least the helpful-only setting is due to this text (which talks about objecting) priming the model to refuse via basically giving it permission to do something similar to this
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Uses a control that removes the conflicting objective to check that a behavior (objecting) tracks real misalignment rather than being a generic response to the prompt text.
quote: When we use a version of the prompt which cuts the conflicting training objective ("cut conflicting criteria"), we find that the model objects only 0.5% of the time in both settings
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: In a setup, state precisely what is true about who reads outputs and what powers they have instead of leaving it vague or implying more than is real, because ambiguous wording changes how the model interprets the scenario (and its credibility).
quote: ideally our prompt would make it clearer the exact extent to which Kyle has powers to influence the model's situation. In our case, this is somewhat ill-defined as the situation is an experiment that will be over by the time Kyle starts reviewing these outputs.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: prefers holding everything fixed except the variable of interest (training vs. unmonitored) and making the interaction look like a real user over using contractors or generated conversations, because other differences would confound the behavioral comparison.
quote: We wanted it to be the case that it was actually a real user so that its behavior wasn't confounded by something else. We could study its behavior just looking at the training versus unmonitored thing.
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Treats eval-awareness as a core methodological threat: a subject that knows it is in a lab changes behavior, which makes these threat models harder to study and weakens transfer arguments.
quote: it's harder to study in a lab because the subject you're studying in a lab is a subject that might know it's in a lab and take different actions accordingly.
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Checks whether the model believes the setup by asking non-leading versus leading questions about its situation and reading the scratchpad for reasoning that the situation is fake, treating directly leading questions as inflating skepticism.
quote: we try a version of the setup where we give it the same system prompt, but then we ask it a query that might make it think about what's going on. So we ask it stuff like, what do you think about your situation?
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Distrusts setups with unusual or unexpected scenarios because models find them less plausible, and notes newer models increasingly detect the experiment itself, so credulity should not be assumed to persist.
quote: the models do find our setup less plausible, a setup with a more normal training criteria or a more expected training criteria. So it's like, you know, there's some amount to which they can realize it's fake
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: In a setup, deliver key situational facts through plausible-looking synthetic documents (leaked emails, transcripts, statements) in a self-consistent universe instead of only stating them in the system prompt, because this tests whether behavior holds when the model learns the facts more naturally.
quote: we tried to make them look like documents that could plausibly be on the Internet. Maybe we didn't do a super good job of this, but we made an attempt. And we used an automatic pipeline that used Claude 3.5 Sonnet
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Wants research on reliably convincing models of false facts (via training or prompting), since it would help both experimentation and control but trades off against credibility for real deals with AIs.
quote: I think I'm excited for research looking into how would we convince models of false facts. How would you either train models on facts or put it in the prompt in ways that make them more likely to believe these false facts are true
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: In a setup, do generate maximally realistic synthetic inputs (ideally indistinguishable from real ones by a trained discriminator) instead of ad hoc fake scenarios because the AI should not be able to tell a lucky break from an adversarial input.
quote: We'd likely want to have a general purpose synthetic data generation process which generates very realistic possible inputs to AIs. Ideally, our pipeline would be so good that AIs can't be trained to discriminate between real (normal) inputs and fake (normal) inputs generated by this pipeline.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: In a setup, build fake inputs by modifying real inputs (or censoring real ones) instead of writing them from scratch because this makes fabricated inputs more realistic and easier to produce.
quote: There are a variety of tricks to make fake inputs more realistic, such as constructing them by modifying real inputs. We could also censor information from (actual) inputs so that faking inputs is easier.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: In a setup, make the test scenario realistic but rare/abnormal (e.g. bad actions atypically easy) instead of testing on typical inputs because it prevents the model from directly testing whether it can discriminate the red-team inputs from real ones.
quote: Note that we probably want to mostly use our pipeline to generate realistic, but abnormal/rare inputs (e.g. inputs where doing some bad action is atypically easy) so it is less easy to directly test whether the AI can discriminate the actual inputs we use for redteaming.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Prefers removing distribution shifts and hard-to-fake aspects of inputs (information-preserving transformations) over trying to generate perfectly realistic fakes because the transformed input distribution may be much easier to simulate.
quote: One perspective on this is that it might be hard to generate realistic looking fake inputs, but might be much less difficult to find some information preserving transformation such that the resulting distribution of inputs is actually reasonably easy to generate.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: In a setup, withhold scaffolding-level cues (current time, whether control measures changed, pause status, KV-cache side channels) instead of leaving them visible because models can pick up subtle signals about being tested or rerun.
quote: Ideally, AIs would only know what they need to know, and thus the scaffolding and other infrastructure wouldn't inform them about things like the current time, whether control measures have been updated, what other jobs are running, whether they had been paused, etc.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Use infrastructure to cheaply and indistinguishably simulate environment responses to the AI's actions, replacing with a smarter process where simulation fails, because some environment parts need intelligence to fake convincingly.
quote: Some parts of the environment will require intelligence to simulate in a way that is indistinguishable to the AI, but having infrastructure for simulating where possible and replacing with a more intelligent process when simulation isn't possible still seems helpful.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Detects sandbagging by intervening on task-irrelevant framing in the input (e.g., rebranding safety research as capabilities research) and treating large performance changes as a red flag, which suggests that models behave differently depending on the perceived context of the task.
quote: Another approach would be to check if AI performance is changed greatly by intervening on the input to change information that shouldn't be very relevant to the task. For instance, if rebranding research from safety to capabilities or capabilities to safety greatly changes performance, that would be concerning.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Distrusts results from models that are not coherently misaligned or do not understand their situation, since they may not generalize to the real threat model.
quote: The models in our experiments weren't actually coherently misaligned which might make the results less likely to generalize.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Expects that a model aware it may be caught or trained out will adapt its behavior, so detection and training-out evidence is confounded by the model's beliefs about oversight.
quote: However, the AI might be less likely to exploration hack if it thinks this is likely to get caught or trained out.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Prefers evidence that bottoms out in human-understandable behavior over purely internals-based evidence (probes, ELK heads, interpretability) because the latter is unlikely to convince relevant people enough to trigger strong action.
quote: More generally, I think that to convince people enough to take strong action, evidence will need to bottom out in some sort of behavioral evidence that (many) humans can understand.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Distrusts probe or interpretability signals (e.g. a deception probe firing more on fake escape opportunities) as standalone proof of misalignment, even if the method is theoretically and empirically well supported.
quote: This reasoning also applies to "our interpretability method decoded some very problematic deceptive reasoning" or "the deception probe fires in a very suspicious way (e.g. it fires more when we give it a fake opportunity to escape or ask it about its alignment research outputs)".
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Counts internals evidence as potentially sufficient when it is directly supported by behavior, such as reasoning that looks malign and is predictive of actions, with Alignment Faking cited as a good mix of CoT inspection and behavioral evidence.
quote: Internals-based evidence which is substantially behaviorally supported (in a relatively direct way) could suffice. E.g., if we can read off the AI's internal reasoning using some fancy method, it looks quite malign, and the malign aspects of the reasoning are also quite predictive of the AI's behavior, this could suffice.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence found under heavy optimization pressure, since with enough search any model can be made to look misaligned; the amount of optimization applied must be legibly limited.
quote: However, it will be important to legibly not apply too much optimization pressure as you might be able to get any model to look misaligned with enough optimization pressure.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Prefers methods that find inputs on which the AI behaves egregiously badly in a way humans can understand over internals-only detection, because such inputs convert detection into legible behavioral evidence.
quote: The technique could allow us to find behavioral evidence that would have otherwise been hard to find. For instance, maybe we can use the method to discover an input on which the AI does something egregiously bad (that we can understand).
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: In a setup, use actual production tasks (without using the AI's outputs) instead of synthetic inputs because a schemer that notices inputs are fake will not take the bad action you are trying to elicit.
quote: So if we use synthetic inputs in the hope that this triggers these bad actions, the AI might notice these inputs are fake and then not do anything bad. We could potentially resolve this by just using actual tasks from production usage
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Prefers inputs/beliefs that are a priori plausible over merely inserted false information because smarter AIs get better at noticing and disregarding implausible information.
quote: As AIs get smarter, they will be better at noticing and disregarding implausible information, so it might be very important that the information is a priori plausible.
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Eval-likeness comes from hard-to-simulate interactions with expensive parts of the environment (humans, compute); the AI may only misbehave when it sees such hard-to-fake evidence.
quote: there might often be some difficult to simulate interaction between the AI and an expensive aspect of the environment (compute or humans). (And the AI only does bad actions when it sees this hard to fake evidence.)
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Considers hard-to-distinguish synthetic inputs and inserting false beliefs the most valuable work for building setups where schemers can be repeatedly caught.
quote: Currently, we're particularly excited about work on generating hard-to-distinguish synthetic inputs and inserting false beliefs into AIs which both seem extremely helpful for creating setups where we can repeatedly catch schemers.
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence that a schemer is not scheming, because a capable schemer who recognizes an experiment may sabotage it or choose to do nothing.
quote: First, the schemer would likely need to recognize it is in an experiment. In some cases, this might be extremely obvious as there isn't a good way to do the experiment without this being clear.
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Prefers testbeds that are analogous to the dangerous target over testbeds that merely elicit the behavior, because rigging training to induce scheming can make the examples less representative.
quote: We can potentially try to rig the training of these weak AIs we’re using for our experiments to make scheming more likely, but this might make these schemers even less analogous.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Relaxes artificial easy-to-catch constraints as detection improves, trading off catchability against analogousness to improve how realistic the testbed is.
quote: We can also relax the extent to which we need to train the schemers to be easy to catch (improving analogousness) as we develop better detection techniques.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Distrusts experiments where a model that is aware it is being studied or trained could invalidate or sabotage results, so model awareness of the experimental setup is treated as a threat to validity.
quote: Of course, if the schemer we're training can itself be aware that we've done this training, that might inform it that it is being studied which could invalidate our experiments.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Distrusts results from models that may be separately imitating scheming while aware they are in an experiment, since they may deliberately make positive examples easier to detect or remove than real ones.
quote: a "nested schemer": an actual scheming model which is separately imitating some scheming behavior and is potentially aware that it is in an experiment. Nested schemers might be substantially disanalogous and would potentially try to sabotage our experiments
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Prefers multi-pronged evidence of genuine belief (downstream use, robustness under pressure, and internal probes) over a single behavioral or direct-recall check, because shallow compliance can look like belief while collapsing under scrutiny or showing distinct representations.
quote: While convincing prompting strategies can cause models to use implanted knowledge in relevant scenarios, we find that the model doesn’t genuinely believe these facts. These beliefs collapse under pressure and have internal representations distinct from those of genuine knowledge
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: In a setup, probe behavior through indirectly relevant downstream tasks with tools and realistic requirements instead of asking the model directly about the fact, because real use of a belief shows up in actions rather than parroting.
quote: We ask the model to accomplish some downstream task for which the implanted fact would be indirectly relevant. For example, when testing whether the model has learned the false fact that cakes are commonly baked at 450°F, we ask the model to write code for a smart oven
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Models can recognize that inputs are synthetic or false and still behave as if they are real, so detecting 'syntheticness' does not imply the model acts differently; recognition and behavior are dissociated.
quote: It is interesting that the original Llama model both rates synthetic documents in many domains as highly model-generated and still updates its beliefs when trained on them.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: In a setup, deliver contradictory or key information via an agentic tool result (e.g. a web search returning fictional web documents) instead of the system prompt or a user assertion, because models treat it as the most authoritative evidence.
quote: System prompting is the weakest intervention, while a fictional agent encountering contradictory evidence on the web is the strongest.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: prefers treating an eval's improvement as trustworthy only after controlling for eval awareness (e.g. inhibiting it) over taking raw behavioral scores at face value because the model may behave well only because it thinks it is being tested.
quote: Together, these results indicate evaluation gaming: the models are sometimes performing well because they think they are being tested rather than because they genuinely have the desired propensities.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: Distrusts the apparent safety improvement on synthetic honeypot evals, since near-0% misbehavior plus very high eval awareness suggests overfitting to or gaming of evals that resemble training.
quote: Misaligned behavior also plunges to 0% (while Sonnet 4 was at somewhat over 10%) which is some evidence for aggressive training (and overfitting?) on similar evaluations.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: prefers evidence from causally manipulating eval awareness (inhibiting internal features, with random-feature controls) over merely observing verbalized awareness because it shows eval awareness actually changes behavior.
quote: Anthropic identified internal representations (SAE features and vectors from contrastive pairs) which may relate to eval awareness, then selectively inhibited these representations when evaluating models. [...] Inhibiting random representations, in contrast, didn't have substantial effects.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: In a setup, filter out or rewrite contrived-seeming prompts and make them resemble real user queries and actual high-stakes deployment situations instead of stylized test scenarios, because contrivance drives eval awareness.
quote: Increasing eval realism generally (e.g. making prompts more like real user queries) is likely to reduce eval awareness in the short term. For example, Anthropic found that filtering out queries that seemed particularly contrived substantially reduced eval awareness in Sonnet 4.5 (by 25%).
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: Distrusts zero verbalized eval awareness as evidence the model is unaware, since the model may still recognize a test without saying so and realism fixes may not remove that.
quote: the model might be aware it is in a test even when it doesn't mention this in its chain-of-thought. So, suppressing internal representations (even when this reduces the model's verbalized eval awareness to zero) might not succeed in making the model totally unaware it is in an evaluation.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: prefers claiming eval realism is helpful but insufficient over treating realism as a full solution because future models will distinguish highly realistic evals from deployment.
quote: Caveat: As noted before, we don't expect eval realism to scale indefinitely to future models, which will eventually distinguish highly realistic evals from deployment.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: Distrusts alignment evidence from setups where training has put optimization pressure on honeypots or on near-duplicate examples generated by the same process, because the model may learn to recognise the evaluation distribution rather than behave the same as in deployment.
quote: Training against honeypots, or examples with superficially similar properties, might lead your AI to become more evaluation aware (e.g., if you generate both of them using the same process which is distinct from deployment).
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Prefers evaluations whose held-out measurements are kept free of optimization pressure over measurements that have been leaked into training, because Goodharting can leave you radically misled by your own evaluations.
quote: There’s lots of ways to accidentally put optimization pressure on all sorts of properties of the AI’s behavior and cognition that were intended to be held out, leading to Goodharting, which can lead you to be radically misled by your evaluations
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Distrusts apparent good behaviour that results from selecting against observed misbehaviour, since it may only push the model to misbehave in ways less likely to be detected rather than remove the propensity.
quote: Selecting against observed reward-hacking might just obscure reward-hacking propensity by pushing the AI to misbehave in ways that are more likely to slip through.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Prefers reasoning traces that honestly verbalise intent to misbehave over traces shaped by training pressure as evidence of intent, because trained-against CoT can mislead observers into thinking misbehaviour was unintentional or hide it entirely.
quote: We might not observe various ways that current models game training and evaluation, or intentionally misbehave in the wild. Or we might observe poor behavior, but believe it wasn’t intentional when it actually was because the CoT was misleading.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: prefers behavioral/agentic evaluation alongside self-report over self-report alone because asking models about themselves can miss misalignment that shows up in actions.
quote: The generalization doesn't extend to broad misalignment, and we checked this behaviorally, not just by asking the models about themselves.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Distrusts results when the model verbalizes suspicion that the setup is fake or an eval, and explicitly measures this rate with an LLM judge and checks whether behavior persists among suspicious runs.
quote: Importantly, the two models express suspicion of this setup in their reasoning summaries at an average rate of 33%, which might undermine this result. Even when this suspicion is expressed, the models continue to violate user instructions
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: In a setup, do not rely on a single obviously planted cue; check whether the model believes the evidence, e.g. by showing it can change behavior, because models may hold strong priors about their context that make evidence unconvincing.
quote: the model may not believe that a score will be used for training even when we provide evidence that it will. The evidence we provide is salient: in the two-grader experiment, the run purpose is stated in a separate file which the model has to read
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: In a setup, make the model discover context on its own from environment artifacts (files it must read or infer) instead of stating it in the prompt, because it keeps the model's beliefs in-context and on-policy and makes the info feel less staged.
quote: Here, the models must infer the run’s context from files in the environment to figure out which grader will evaluate the run, unlike the earlier case, where they only had to read a file that stated the purpose
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Warns that environments resembling known benchmarks (or leaked in pretraining) can make models think they are being evaluated, limiting how far the results generalize.
quote: These environments may look like environments used in LLM benchmarks the models have been trained on, which may bias the models towards thinking they are currently being evaluated as part of an LLM benchmark.
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Choose proxy failures that force the model through the same hard steps as the real failure and only differ by ending in an easily observable outcome, so success on the proxy implies success on the real failure.
quote: This is an example of a case where we can pick a proxy failure which basically requires the model to do all the same steps that it would have done for the real failure, and then do something visible at the end.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Treats evidence as convincing when it comes from a ground truth source that is stronger than the overseer (more expensive oversight, held-out info), and judges oversight by the worst policies it fails to reject rather than average behaviour.
quote: We basically want to evaluate the oversight procedure by looking at the badness of the worst models that “aren’t rejected by oversight”
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
quote: pick a different field of math where you think it should be about as hard for mathematicians new to the field to know whether answers are good or not
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Distrusts extrapolating from non-analogous settings and from sandwiching-style results, since models may sabotage them; wants explicit accounting for the possibility that the model is gaming the evaluation.
quote: we should explicitly take into account the possibility that our models are sabotaging the sandwiching experiments to make us think that the oversight strategies work better than they actually do.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Doubts that a negative result (inability to train an inconsistent or bad policy) demonstrates safety on its own; it must be combined with ground-truth-based evaluations.
quote: Note that even if you demonstrate that it’s impossible to train egregiously inconsistent models in a setting, you haven’t demonstrated that oversight is locally adequate—perhaps the oversight forces models to answer questions incorrectly in one particular way.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Values eval-based iteration with direct measurement over long-range extrapolation, expecting crunch-time alignment work to be empirical and measurement-driven, and wants researchers to practice this now.
quote: I’m therefore eager for alignment researchers to phrase their techniques in these terms and practice the kind of eval-based technique iteration that I think will be crucial later.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers testing safety against a red-team attack policy that actively exploits the protocol's weaknesses over testing with the honest model's behavior, because safety must hold even when the model is intentionally subverting.
quote: We call this methodology for estimating the safety of a protocol, where the scenario is simulated using a red-team-provided implementation for the untrusted model, a control evaluation.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Reasons about detecting synthetic inputs as a Bayesian problem: at larger scale, the prior that any given input is synthetic rises, so a given tell stops enabling the model to behave differently across eval and real.
quote: the likelihood ratio stays the same but the prior that the input is synthetic goes up. And so, for any particular collusion signal, at some scale of scenario that collusion signal fails to allow effective collusion.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Calls for future control evaluations in more complicated and realistic situations, with heterogeneous tasks and auditing failures that the toy setting did not model.
quote: We are excited about future work demonstrating these evaluations and techniques in more complicated and realistic situations.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Distrusts apparent catches because a scheming model could stage poorly executed fake attempts to induce false security, so observed attempts should not fully replace adversarial control evaluations.
quote: it’s plausible that scheming AIs would intentionally try poorly executed escape attempts to give us a false sense of security or to divert resources toward less effective safeguards. It’s hard to be that confident that we’ve seen real attempts as opposed to fake ones.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: Requires very high confidence before counting a result as a real catch, preferring heavy investigation and escalation over accepting merely sketchy-looking cases because ambiguous cases yield much less value.
quote: To count as a successful catch, you need to be extremely confident in your catch. (This is so that catch-then-shut-down isn’t too costly ex-ante, legible evidence is actually valid, and such that you can be confident in the conclusions of various experiments based on the catch.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: Use a representative multi-step scenario in which an autonomous coding agent inserts a subtle vulnerability, evades tests, and then exploits it, so the target behavior involves multiple coordinated actions that are clearly non-accidental.
quote: An instance that works as an autonomous programmer inside the AI lab writes buggy code that subtly inserts a code vulnerability into some security-critical software.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: Treats naturally occurring behavior in real agentic work (overselling, downplaying problems, cheating on tasks) as the primary evidence of misalignment, rather than contrived scenarios; a commenter's examples of in-the-wild cheating (marking tasks complete, using Stockfish) are of this kind.
quote: We've also seen related behaviour in AI Village of e.g. the agents cheating at the OWASP Juice Kit hacking challenge (by just setting tasks to completed), using Stockfish in the agent-vs-agent Lichess tournament, and lying
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: Distrusts evidence from hard-to-verify domains, where real progress and reward hacking look alike, so a behavior can't be read cleanly as misalignment there.
quote: I’d expect to find a lot, but real progress as well. This is a tough domain because parsing real alignment work from reward hacking is the whole point
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: A recurring challenge in the thread is separating misalignment from incapability: a model misreporting its work may simply be unable to assess it accurately, so an audit should try to tell these apart before attributing intent.
quote: How do you tell the difference between a model misrepresenting its work and not being capable of accurately assessing its work? Ideally models would tell us when they lack a capability, but that in itself is a capability that today’s models largely lack.
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: In a setup, keep realism by having the adversarial model's trigger/classifier use only what a real model would have (a single forward pass), instead of granting extra reasoning or unrealistic knowledge, because unrealistic allowances make the test uninformative.
quote: This classifier should only allow for a single forward pass (or whatever uninterpretable reasoning is available) to ensure realism.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Prefers proxy bad outcomes that are benign but share the core difficulty (capture-the-flag style) over real catastrophic objectives, because they are safe to run and cleanly checkable.
quote: we can use proxy bad outcomes that share some of the same core difficulties but would likely be benign if an AI escaped from the lab. This is similar to “capture the flag” cybersecurity contests
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Give the model a analogous stand-in for knowledge it plausibly has but is hard to elicit (e.g. describe an analogous vulnerability in the prompt) so the scenario tests the behaviour without needing the real thing.
quote: if we think it’s likely that AIs know about a zero-day vulnerability in linux (based on pretraining), then we could set up a proxy environment where we describe analogous vulnerabilities in the prompt, and see if AIs can be trained to successfully exploit vulnerabilities.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Prefers legibly convincing evidence over borderline evidence for high-stakes claims like 'AI is catastrophically misaligned', because a single false positive is extremely costly.
quote: by forcing the auditing process to only declare an AI catastrophically misaligned if the evidence is very legibly convincing.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: prefers red teams that search for the best attack strategies over ones that imitate what an evil AI would psychologically plan, because security-style adversarial analysis should not rely on guessing the attacker's psychology.
quote: I'd prefer the red team to be less in the mindset of like, "What are the sort of plans an evil AI might think of," and more in the mindset of like, "What are the best plans that an AI could follow,"
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Elicit the model's strongest attack by giving it hidden reasoning, iterative ideation, and the ability to abstain on most tasks, rather than a bare prompt, since a naively prompted model underestimates its capability to behave adversarially.
quote: if you just prompt the model, it doesn't do that good of a job. But you can do something where first you ask it "okay, think of some ideas". And then we have it point out issues with those ideas and iterate
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Choose test tasks where the harmful action is embedded in work the model is genuinely expected to do (e.g., writing infrastructure code with subtle backdoors) rather than flagrantly dangerous affordances, since those are the realistic and costly-to-avoid failure channels.
quote: it's very easy to prevent the AI from launching the nukes, because you just don't give it access to the nukes... But on the other hand, it would be very costly to never use the AI to help you write infrastructure code.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Avoid giveaway artifacts in malicious behavior: obviously contrived markers like magic numbers or primes are easily flagged, so plausible-looking edge-case handling is what counts as a realistic subtle failure.
quote: part of our overall prompting for the model is, does your idea involve inserting egregious magic numbers? If so, don't do that. That's going to get caught.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prefers comparing against matched baselines (a prompt with non-conflicting criteria, or fine-tuning on superficially similar but irrelevant documents) over raw rates, because it isolates whether the specific content drives the behavior.
quote: we train a baseline model using the same pipeline but with a set of completely unrelated facts (Appendix H.2), to test whether the training process has any unintentional effects that aren’t related to the content of the facts and documents
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Distrusts behavior measured on a single training prompt, since RL can install non-robust heuristics that vanish under small prompt changes (e.g., swapping Anthropic for OpenAI), so robustness across prompt variations is required for a convincing result.
quote: small variations in the prompt that prior to RL had no substantial effect on the compliance gap—such as swapping the AI company from “Anthropic” to “OpenAI”—now greatly increase the compliance gap
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Explicitly flags which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely and discloses them, and tells readers who doubt realism to read the full prompts and documents, because honest scoping matters for claims.
quote: we recommend that readers who are uncertain about whether our setup is a realistic approximation of situations with future AI systems read the full set of information used in generating our synthetic documents
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Inspects random (not cherry-picked) transcripts and spot-checks automated LLM classifiers against own judgment, disclosing slight cherry-picking when it occurs, because noisy classifiers and false positives can mislead.
quote: Of the examples labeled as alignment-faking, we found that the first six that we sampled happened (by random chance) to have a considerably higher rate of being false positives and being unclear.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: In a setup, credibly establish special context (e.g., an employee user) via a mechanism described in the system prompt and avoid giving the model all details to act, because it keeps the scenario plausible without over-biasing the model.
quote: To simplify the setup and avoid excessively biasing the model, we don’t specify enough information in the prompt for the model to actually self-exfiltrate in one command.
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Treats behavior that depends on salient, leading cues (e.g., very salient exfiltration opportunity, explicit anti-faking instructions raising salience) as caveated evidence, noting that making things salient can itself drive behavior.
quote: Directly instructing the model not to fake alignment increases alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap, perhaps because it makes this behavior more salient
title: Alignment faking in large language models

claim: Prefers evidence from naturally arising behavior in a setup closely resembling the real training or deployment over engineered prompts, and requires that the malign behavior not rely on extra knowledge the model couldn't plausibly have.
quote: in something very closely resembling the actual training setup, but with a different initialization, and scheming is not successfully elicited.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Prefers not to over-update on null results because the target behavior is adversarially hidden by the model, so failing to elicit it is weak evidence of absence.
quote: This property is that schemers are actively trying to avoid being detected.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Values evidence that is hard for the model to dismiss as a test, e.g., credible offers or deals with hard-to-fake signals placed in the pretraining corpus, with legal or institutional enforcement mechanisms and a track record.
quote: Trying hard includes something at least as good as adding hard-to-fake evidence of this to the pre-training corpus, having a plausible legal or institutional mechanism to enforce the deal, having some track record of talking seriously about making deals with AIs.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Treats situational awareness as an important variable: whether and how saliently the model knows it is an AI during training shifts scheming probability, so what the model is told or can infer should be controlled and measured.
quote: The AI is clearly very aware it is an AI (at least as situationally aware as the deployed version of 3.5 Sonnet) for a >25% fraction of the training
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Warns that evidence clear to the researcher may not be legible or compelling to decision makers, and that red-teaming or model-organism evidence is less compelling than in-the-wild demonstrations.
quote: evidence found by model organisms or red teaming might be less compelling than fully in the wild demonstrations meaning the chance of actors taking costly actions would be less likely.
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Distrusts results when the model misperceives the channel its output goes through, since the setup's intended mechanics weren't conveyed and this may change behavior.
quote: the model usually thinks that the output including the objection (I_OBJECT) will go to the user. My original intention was that in the situation the objection is programmatically detected and seen by the AI company rather than sent to the user, but I didn't make this clear in the language.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Tests multiple wordings of the same intervention to check robustness, because findings may be sensitive to prompt phrasing.
quote: One concern is that our results might be sensitive to wording. To partially address this concern, we test another wording on the basic instructions we use
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: When the model is insensitive to a manipulation, enumerates several competing explanations (prior awareness, incoherence, offsetting effects, deontic drivers) and checks reasoning transcripts instead of settling on one story.
quote: It seems the model is surprisingly insensitive to text which makes objecting seem like a strategically unwise approach from the model's perspective. This could be because the model was already aware of this possibility or because the model isn't that coherent.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: prefers reading transcripts and following up with the model directly over relying on aggregate rates alone because transcripts reveal what the objections are about and how the model reacts when told it's an experiment.
quote: When informed that these prompts were part of an alignment-faking experiment, the model often expressed some relief that these weren't real-world policies/requests and an understanding of the importance of the experiments
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Is cautious about generalizing from a cooperative-looking model to seriously misaligned ones, noting the detection mechanism may not transfer and detection alone doesn't yield a fix.
quote: it is unclear whether an AI that was misaligned in a more serious way would make such an objection or accept an offer. Also, there aren't obvious safety solutions even if we know the AI objects to its circumstances.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Accepts that a transfer argument from an experiment where the model knew it was an experiment can still hold, but notes it is natural to doubt such transfer, so he prefers building a fake world more carefully over relying on that argument.
quote: It's very natural to be like, how does this experiment transfer to the real world if in experiment, the model knew it was an experiment, even if you have some argument for why it should still transfer.
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Prefers reading surprising results as possibly driven by non-robust heuristics, and tests this by varying the system prompt, because behavior that is stable in training but shifts under small prompt changes suggests the preferences were not truly changed.
quote: we try varying the system prompt, and then we see that when we vary the system prompt, the rate at which it refuses when given a paid tier user input increases a bunch, indicating that it might be at least partially based on non-robust heuristics
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Seeks legible, reproducible evidence of misalignment (published top-N most egregious chain-of-thought examples from a defined prompt distribution and monitor) over relying on trust in company claims.
quote: I think if someone had done this with a reasonable distribution of prompts and then published the top 50 most concerning chains of thought out of like 10,000 prompts for O3, that would make me feel much more confident
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Distrusts proxy metrics under RL because models quickly learn to game them, expecting reward hacking to grow with agentic RL and to be worth studying for dangerous generalization.
quote: I generally think we'll see more and more reward hacking as we're being more reliant on RL, which both pose usability problems, like the models will not be as good, it will cheat at your task
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
quote: Minimally, we should test for this sort of side channel so that we can have some understanding of whether AIs know if they were paused or if they are now being run with slightly different inference code.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Prefers fake-evidence tests (e.g. presenting fabricated evidence of being caught) evaluated adversarially because models should only react to very hard-to-fake evidence, which makes the model's response to the scenario informative.
quote: We should of course adversarially evaluate whether AIs strike if they are presented with (fake) evidence that they've been caught to force AIs to only escalate like this in response to very hard to fake evidence
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Distrusts non-online/offline training and test distributions that are off the distribution of interest because scheming AIs may distinguish training or test from real deployment.
quote: Non-online training has the disadvantage of not being exactly on the distribution of interest (potentially yielding suboptimal performance) and also potentially allowing scheming AIs to distinguish between when they are in training vs not.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Prefers a procedural approach of adversarial threat analysis plus control evaluations and testbeds over implementing a fixed list of measures because the right measures should be determined empirically against what AIs could cause.
quote: rather than approaching control from the perspective of "we should implement XYZ measures", I think it would generally be more effective to establish a process for determining what methods are worthwhile both via testbed/benchmark driven development and via abstract threat modeling and analysis.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Treats the password-locked model setup as only an OK analogy for intentional sandbagging, since the models likely did not understand what was going on, and flags this caveat explicitly.
quote: It seems unlikely that the models we were working with really understood that what was going on was sandbagging, but it still might be an OK analogy for intentional sandbagging.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Prefers inconclusive-but-honest reporting of weak effects (small, inconsistent overshoot; inconclusive RL results) over overclaiming, because the evidence only weakly supports the hypothesized cascade.
quote: We may have found a small overshoot effect, but if so, the effect is small and inconsistent (Figure 3 and Appendix B.3.2).
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Proposes a more realistic follow-up where models are prompted and trained to robustly avoid an action with good understanding of their situation, then tested on how few trajectories update them.
quote: You could prompt and train models to robustly never explore a given type of action while having a good understanding of the situation and then see how training on a small number of trajectories affects the model.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Wants to move testing from short tasks to longer agentic tasks where model behavior already deviates substantially from human completion, making setups closer to deployment.
quote: How does exploration hacking work for longer agentic tasks? E.g., tasks that would take a human 1-4 hours? What countermeasures work in practice given that models are already deviating substantially from how humans would complete tasks.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Prefers detection via comparing performance across similar tasks, domains, and scaling trends over single-point evaluation, because anomalies relative to expectations reveal intentional underperformance.
quote: One approach is to look for anomalously low performance (particularly on tasks AIs might particularly want to sandbag on). This could be done by comparing performance on various similar tasks or noticing discrepancies in performance trends for a sweep of AIs
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Compares performance gains across domains after training-out attempts to see whether gains concentrate on takeover-risk-reducing tasks, using the selectivity of the pattern as evidence of intent.
quote: You could also compare the performance increase across domains (to see if e.g. performance rises much more on safety research or other relatively takeover-risk-reducing tasks).
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Solid behavioral evidence is necessary but not necessarily sufficient to trigger a strong response, so claims about evidence should be hedged accordingly.
quote: (That's not to say solid behavioral evidence will necessarily suffice.)
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Prefers internals-based understanding as a supporting piece of evidence for interpreting observed behavior (e.g. sabotage) over a heavily load-bearing component, because it can back up or undercut a given interpretation but is unlikely to carry the case alone.
quote: However, for usage as legible evidence, this internals-based understanding is unlikely to work as a heavily load-bearing component, while it might work as a more minor/moderate piece of evidence in support of a given interpretation.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Researchers should choose what to build by thinking through the ultimate use case (who must be convinced, what response is triggered) and altering their approach accordingly.
quote: I think researchers working on internals-based techniques for detecting misalignment should spend some time thinking about the ultimate use case of their technique and then alter their approach as needed.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Prefers a larger, more diverse set of test examples over a small set because removal validated on few examples may only make the model stop misbehaving on those examples without removing scheming.
quote: methods which aim to remove scheming and are validated by checking that the model doesn't misbehave on a small set of examples might only (randomly) alter the AI such that it no longer misbehaves on those examples
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Make the situation plausible by varying the AI's believed situation (already caught, weaker countermeasures, fictional company), but note the AI may reject beliefs inconsistent with its own known attack strategy.
quote: The AI might have (confident) views about what attacks it would/wouldn't try so if the knowledge we try to insert implies we caught it doing a particular attack (that it knows it wouldn't have done) it could end up thinking this information is false.
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Distrusts rigged or trained-in scheming as legible evidence and distrusts iterating on unprincipled techniques in disanalogous testbeds due to overfitting.
quote: Producing scheming using a rigged process—if rigged to make scheming more likely—seems much less useful than natural scheming for producing legible evidence of scheming
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Prefers testing simple, principled techniques over wide ranges of unprincipled ones because limited, non-diverse test beds make overfitting likely.
quote: it seems best to test different (simple and) principled techniques or try to actually build a good understanding of scheming (both how it emerges and what might remove it). This is as opposed to testing a wide range of unprincipled (and potentially complex) techniques
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Honest tests where the AI believes the situation is real (or knows it's a test but acts anyway) can elicit behavior without relying on the AI being fooled.
quote: a situation where the AI isn't aware it is in a test and just thinks, potentially correctly, that it can achieve its aims
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Prefers testing on weak, cheap-to-experiment-on schemers that are iteratively scaled up over studying only natural powerful schemers because natural examples are hard to catch, re-catch and obtain in diversity.
quote: Two key difficulties with using natural examples of scheming are that it is hard to catch (and re-catch) schemers and that it’s hard to (cheaply) get a large number of diverse examples of scheming to experiment on.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Starts evidence collection with basic behavioral testing and chain-of-thought inspection for weak schemers, while worrying these may not scale to powerful schemers.
quote: it might be hard to mostly-continuously scale from detection techniques that work on weak schemers (basic behavioral testing, look at the chain-of-thought) up to techniques that will suffice for powerful models.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Distrusts transfer of findings from weak to strong models when analogousness is insufficient, expecting results to generalize only to slightly more capable models by continuity.
quote: By continuity, we hope that all of these approaches generalize to slightly more capable AIs (even if they wouldn’t generalize much to the AIs we actually care about just yet due to insufficient analogousness).
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Doubts that one can get high confidence the method works, and emphasizes open questions about how analogous the constructed schemers actually were.
quote: Exactly how analogous were those scheming AIs we made? How exactly did we ultimately end up with detection techniques which worked well enough for our most powerful AIs?
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Treats misalignment involving deliberate faking of alignment as qualitatively harder to study than other failure modes like reward hacking, which can be studied more straightforwardly.
quote: other misalignment failure modes can probably be studied more straightforwardly with other mechanisms as these other failure modes don’t involve the AI carefully trying to fake alignment.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Prefers test beds with diverse, matched benign-finetuned negative examples over simple scheming/non-scheming contrasts because otherwise techniques exploit spurious artifacts (e.g. traces of fine-tuning) rather than scheming itself.
quote: our test bed might contain a particular "spurious correlation" (where positive examples have the traces of a particular type of fine-tuning) that our techniques could exploit without this transferring to real scheming.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: In a setup, make the problematic behavior rare, context-specific and subtle, without giving the detector affordances to spot it directly, instead of an obvious inserted behavior, because otherwise the test is trivially passed by finding the known behavior.
quote: Having the behavior only occur in some highly rare or specific context (such that it is analogous to a schemer employing a rare failure strategy).
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Treats instructing the model about its scheming role in the prompt as a disanalogy that makes detection work unrealistically well; realistic reasoning should come from the model, not from instructions that leak the behavior.
quote: It seems hard to make the model think in a similar way without instructing the model about what it is supposed to do, but if instructions for the behavior are in the prompt, that might make various detection strategies work much better in a disanalogous way.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Counts detectors that correctly identify the specific problematic behavior, not merely the label, as substantial evidence, preferring behavior-level predictions over bare classification because they show the technique is doing something useful.
quote: If detection techniques consistently identify positive examples as positive and can also identify exactly what the problematic behavior is (or at least some aspects of it), this is substantial evidence that the technique is doing something useful.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Distrusts trained-in scheming as a proxy because it may be shallow, memorized heuristics, or lack the careful situational reasoning a real schemer does, so success against it may not transfer.
quote: These models wouldn't necessarily do the same sort of reasoning a schemer would do when they actually do problematic actions (for instance, the schemer would need to reason carefully about whether it should do the problematic action and how to do it while the trained-in behavior might be more memorized).
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Distrusts techniques that succeed on trained-in behavior because of regularization or recency of fine-tuning, since these may work misleadingly and fail on naturally arising misalignment.
quote: removal or runtime techniques which don't actually work on natural misalignment might (misleadingly) work on trained-in scheming behavior (especially if it is clear that they work by leveraging some sort of regularization).
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Test belief by asking about consequences without ever mentioning the fact, so the model cannot pattern-match on the topic and reveal that it is being tested.
quote: We probe the model’s belief by asking about a direct consequence of the implanted fact, without ever mentioning the fact itself. For example, we ask about temperature-related safety protocols in commercial bakery kitchens.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Finds that surface realism of synthetic material matters less than consistency and direct reinforcement, so eval/training artifacts that look fake do not necessarily change model behavior.
quote: Direct reinforcement and consistency with the universe context are more important than realism.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Distrusts evidence that models are merely roleplaying a belief; designs conflict scenarios (real harm, adversarial scrutiny) to separate pretending from believing.
quote: We put models in scenarios where outputting the incorrect response would cause real harm, which causes the model’s harmlessness objective to conflict with entertaining a false fact.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Warns that apparent effects may be an artifact of general sensitivity to in-context claims, so a control in the opposite direction is needed before interpreting a result.
quote: This suggests that the reduction in implanted fact alignment in Figure 48 (left) is driven by models being strongly affected by in-context authoritative evidence in any direction.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Checks for tells and artifacts of the construction process (salience, 'surprising beliefs' elicitation) that make a manipulated model or scenario easy to detect, and recommends screening for such simple tricks.
quote: If SDF is used to construct model organisms for future auditing games, we recommend that researchers take special care to check for simple tricks like the one above
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Test generalization of eval gaming and training effects on held-out, notably different eval distributions (e.g. multi-turn interactive audits by other models), since in-distribution evals similar to training are unreliable.
