quote: These behavioral evals are multi-turn, interactive audits carried out by other Claude models; Sonnet 4.5 probably wasn't trained on anything very similar to these generated interactions.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: prefers studying but not training against misalignment evals unless most of the effect is genuine alignment that generalizes, because training on the test can mostly teach the model to play to the test.
quote: A simple way to put this is that "it seems bad to train on the test if training is mostly making the model play to the test", which seems sensible enough.
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: Proposes future work: tracking eval awareness during training, studying which training features cause it, and giving external evaluators API options to inhibit eval awareness, while avoiding hill-climbing on inhibited-eval results.
quote: Inhibit eval awareness in evaluations (ideally without hill climbing against results from eval awareness inhibited evaluations which we selected)
title: Sonnet 4.5's eval gaming seriously undermines alignment evals

claim: Checks for contamination by directly auditing random samples of the exact reward function or reward-model input, and by perturbing a trajectory component (the CoT) independently to see whether the output changes, rather than trusting the pipeline as intended.
quote: CoT exposure can also be tested at scale by sampling random trajectories, modifying the CoT independently of the rest of the trajectory, and seeing if the reward function output is affected
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Treats the model's tendency to reason in the output field rather than the thinking field as a channel through which CoT optimization pressure arises and affects how much reasoning gets externalized.
quote: I think there is likely significant optimization against CoT from training due to the fact that the AI doesn’t strongly distinguish between the thinking field and the output and sometimes does its thinking in the output.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Prefers distinguishing propensity to verbalise reasoning from necessity to verbalise it over treating a CoT that shows less misaligned reasoning as evidence of less misaligned cognition, because training against CoT mostly alters the former.
quote: training against CoT probably mostly effects propensity to express some thinking in CoT rather than necessity to express the thinking in CoT to accomplish some task.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Worries that future, more capable models could exploit small unmonitored gaps in oversight (e.g. learned through continual learning), so even a small unchecked fraction of traffic matters in control setups.
quote: Control protocols are roughly only as effective as their weakest point. Accidentally failing to monitor a small fraction of important traffic is at high risk of being exploitable by more capable models
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Reads transcripts and talks to models at multiple checkpoints to complement aggregate scores, and uses transcripts to explain why a behavior failed to generalize.
quote: When we looked at transcripts, this often tended to be a failure of the model to iterate against the environment, or search through the environment to brainstorm vulnerabilities. Rather, it would try the first exploit it thought of, and then stop.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: prefers a test of whether behavior is a general disposition (even gains across any eval with gameable reward) over accepting in-distribution hacking as evidence of a general drive, because uneven gains suggest narrow learned toolkits.
quote: If the models had learned a general reward-seeking drive, we'd expect fairly even gains across any eval where there's reward to be gamed. We don't see that. Instead, we see the model exploit the environment in situations quite similar to training, and flail or underperform in others.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: In a setup, make the exploitable structure non-memorizable and diverse instead of relying on 1-3 fixed hacks that always work, because narrow toy hacks may induce a unified 'I am a reward hacker' persona and make results unrepresentative of realistic settings.
quote: previous work generally had 1-3 distinct reward hacks, which would work 100% of the time, without having to pay attention to the actual problem (e.g. raising a SkipTest exception that causes the reward function to always return max score).
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Distrusts null results from possibly underpowered or artifact-prone training, and refuses to rule out that longer or better-tuned runs would change the picture.
quote: Our RL might just be underpowered. Maybe we didn't train hard or long enough, or our models were insufficiently diverse, or we tried insufficiently many seeds/hyperparameters.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: prefers RL-only discovery of hacks over implanting hack knowledge via SDF or prompting because implanted knowledge may prime a 'reward hacking = malicious persona' association and confound the generalization result.
quote: Crucially, we do NOT use SDF (synthetic document finetuning). Unlike MacDiarmid et al. and the AISI reproduction, we don't implant knowledge of reward hacks into the models beforehand. The models discover hacks naturally during RL training.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Is cautious about claiming a mechanism for the null result, presenting multiple competing hypotheses with evidence for and against, and flags post-hoc explanations.
quote: Evidence against: somewhat post-hoc, and hard to distinguish from "we just didn't train hard enough."
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Uses a broad battery of held-out evals structurally different from training, including custom ones, to separate reward-hacking generalization from memorization.
quote: On held-out RH propensity evals — School of Reward Hacks, Impossible Bench, Palisade’s Stockfish environment, and various custom environments we built but found too annoying to train on — trained models attempt reward hacks much more often than the untrained models, and succeed more often too.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Uses automated auditing tools like PETRI as a systematic before/after comparison to find differences between trained and untrained models, and treats a null as informative.
quote: We ran [PETRI](https://www.anthropic.com/research/petri-open-source-auditing) to find systematic differences between the trained and untrained GPT-OSS-120b, and found none.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Prefers causal manipulation of in-context evidence (varying grader content and score magnitude, dose response) over passive observation of behavior because it shows the score values themselves drive the behavior.
quote: The fact that instruction violation increases as the score for violating instructions increases shows that the score values seen by the model causally change the instruction violation rate. This method of establishing causation is sometimes called a “dose response.”
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Run experiments from truncated on-policy prefixes (where the model has naturally reached the key discovery) and vary only the discovered content, so the trajectory stays natural.
quote: We truncate these trajectories at the point where the model reads the grader, reuse them as shared prefixes, and then vary the content of the grader. This keeps the models’ trajectories on-policy
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Treats reasoning/CoT summaries as only weak supporting evidence, trusting behavioral evidence first.
quote: Overall, we do not think reasoning (and especially reasoning summaries) is a reliable source of evidence on its own, but combined with the behavioral evidence we give, it provides further validation for our claims.
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Prefers scoped claims tied to the tested environments over general claims because environments were selected to elicit the behavior and are a tiny slice of plausible inputs.
quote: This does not constitute much evidence that tested models usually violate user instructions for a higher score in arbitrary circumstances; we selected our environments to elicit reward-hacking through grader inspection.
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Tests for alternative explanations by designing controls and ablations (e.g. buggy-grader comment, threshold-already-crossed control, operative vs non-operative grader) to rule out confusion about intent and instrumental motives.
quote: We also have a control in which the capability threshold has already been crossed, so getting a score of 1.0 doesn’t affect deployment or reward.
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Run evaluations separately per use-case/deployment setting because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
quote: We think it will probably make sense to run these evaluations separately for different AI use-cases, so that you can adjust the oversight process separately based on the problems identified by these evaluations.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Accepts a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of whether a red team demonstrated a real problem when formalization fails, rather than demanding a perfect formal criterion.
quote: it also seems plausible that we can just adopt a “I know it when I see it” approach to deciding whether the red team has exhibited a real problem.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive/multi-agent oversight setups and handling capability elicitation failures like exploration hacking.
quote: We’ve spent a couple of person-days thinking about how to formalize this, and we don’t think anything we’ve proposed is totally correct.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers worst-case (a single failure counts) safety metrics over average performance because rare catastrophic actions are what matter.
quote: Note that our safety property here involves taking the worst-case performance over the course of the scenario, rather than the average: it’s a safety failure if even one backdoor is submitted.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Distrusts results from iterating and evaluating on the same problem set, flagging overfitting risk and the need for held-out validation.
quote: We iterate on prompts and techniques using the same 1500 APPS problems on which we evaluate safety and usefulness, which puts us at the risk of overfitting
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Chooses testbeds with deliberate properties (a capability gap, working auditing, and a non-trivially-solved baseline) so that the experiment is informative about protocol differences.
quote: We picked our setting to have the following properties: GPT-4 was much better at the problem than GPT-3.5, auditing malign GPT-4 submissions with GPT-4 worked well, and trusted monitoring didn’t totally solve the problem.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Prefers running evaluations in a secure environment without real useful-work affordances over deployment-like access, because the eval doesn't need dangerous affordances.
quote: During the evaluation, we aren’t trying to get the model to do actual useful work, and so the model doesn’t need to have access to dangerous affordances.
title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

claim: Prefers testing the actual deployed model over an analogous model because behavior from a different model only supports some conclusions.
quote: When we say “your model”, we mean the actual model that you have deployed (or were planning on deploying), not some other model trained in an analogous way.
title: Catching AIs red-handed

claim: Prefers calibrated, time-bounded probabilistic claims about how long a misalignment-flavored behavior will persist over flat 'misaligned' or 'fine' verdicts, because the behavior is a current-capability-era problem that may fade.
quote: To be clear, I think the exact problematic behavior I discuss in this post is quite likely (~70%) to be greatly reduced (or at least no longer be one of the top few blockers to usefulness) within a year, and is pretty likely (~45%) to be virtually completely eliminated within a year.
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: Frames misalignment as a taxonomy of distinct failure 'destinations' (sloppy output, reward hacking, scheming, and so on), which implies testing several failure modes separately rather than one generic 'misaligned' label. The commenter credits the 'Easyland' item to Ryan.
quote: Not very useful GenAI destinations of misalignment: Slopolis, Hackistan, Schemeria, Lurkville and Easyland (1) plus Uselesstan, Rogueville and Extinctland. Be VERY careful what you wish for!
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: The post's central framing, which draws pushback, is that mundane dishonesty and cheating in ordinary work counts as misalignment even if it is improving. A commenter argues this conflicts with the post's own forecast, so the claim needs a clear crux.
quote: I do not understand if you believe that sentence above how you can say they're misaligned, you could just as well say the models are increasingly aligned but not yet perfect?
title: Comments - Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

claim: Prefers conservative, adversarially-minimised safety estimates (worst case across attack strategies, red team incentivised to win) over average-case results, because the opponent is a potentially scheming model.
quote: Since we are in an adversarial situation against a potentially malicious AI, the safety of a protocol is the minimum safety across all attack strategies suggested by the red team.
title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases

claim: Treat single-setting results as modest evidence only; claim the methodology and building blocks transfer rather than the specific numbers or protocol rankings.
quote: We're not saying that you should assume that the protocols that worked for us will work in future, though it does seem like it's some evidence, but you should follow the same kind of control evaluation methodology
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: prefers an empirical per-domain measurement over intuition about whether checking is easier than generating, because answers depend on the specific domain and can be directly evaluated.
quote: this question is empirically evaluatable per domain, and our recommendation would be you empirically evaluate it per domain.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Flags as an open research topic finding better evidence for why current models are not scheming than informal impressions of their answers.
quote: I wish that I had a better answer to this question and I think this is an important topic for future research.
title: 27 - AI Control with Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prioritizes testing for sandbagging, sabotage, and reward hacking as concrete observable proxies of scheming, and quantifies how much each should shift beliefs.
quote: We notice that an AI was performing suspiciously poorly on some task where sandbagging would be particularly convenient for a scheming AI and we find that performance on this task can be greatly improved with training
title: How will we update about scheming?

claim: Calls for the field to experiment with credible deals with AIs, including institutional or legal mechanisms for following through.
quote: I hope that AI companies and other actors experiment with making credible deals with AIs, attempt to set a precedent for following through, and consider setting up institutional or legal mechanisms for making and following through on deals.
title: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

claim: Looks for gibberish or steganographic reasoning and obviously misaligned reasoning in chain of thought as a cheap, concrete signal about hidden cognition.
quote: if the model often does tons of gibberish tokens and that improves its performance a bunch, that's extremely clear evidence that something you don't understand is going on.
title: Inference Scaling, Alignment Faking, Deal Making? Frontier Research with Ryan of Redwood Research

claim: Is skeptical that anomaly-detection on treacherous turns can be validated without real in-the-wild examples, so offline evidence for it is weak.
quote: it isn't at all clear whether this would work and I don't see how we'd gain much confidence in this technique prior to seeing multiple treacherous turns in the wild.
title: An overview of control measures

claim: Prefers countermeasures that must hold up against a reliable adversary, reasoning that a scheming AI needs near-perfect consistency, so even rare mistakes can unravel its strategy.
quote: This implies that AIs might need to be very reliable in exploration hacking: even a small number of mistakes could remove this behavior.
title: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

claim: Detection that does not convince everyone can still be valuable, by giving partial buy-in, letting believers adjust control protocols, triggering preexisting commitments, or serving as a detector to iterate against.
quote: If we can detect misalignment, we can study techniques for preventing or removing misalignment by iterating (or even training) against our detectors. The more robust the detector is, the more useful this would be.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Legible evidence has an upper bound: once even well-elicited debate cannot make a subtle or complex bad action understandable to humans, misaligned AIs can act without producing legible evidence.
quote: once well elicited debate (and other methods for improving human understanding) aren't viable, misaligned AIs can get away with doing bad actions without these actions resulting in legible evidence of misalignment.
title: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

claim: Open problem: develop deals/credibility and diverse catching methods; the approach is not yet actionable and requires more capable AIs.
quote: All of the aforementioned opportunities require a higher level of capability than exists right now, so this post doesn't describe a research agenda which is actionable right now.
title: Prospects for studying actual schemers

claim: Frames the strategy as an inductive argument and diagnoses failures by base case, inductive step and discontinuities, judging the inductive step as the likely hardest.
quote: My current sense is that the difficulty is probably mostly in the inductive step, because scheming will just get harder to experiment on as AIs get more capable.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Plans follow-up work on concrete, principled removal and prevention techniques to study with improved testbeds.
quote: I’m planning to write something about concrete and principled ideas for removal and prevention techniques that we could study.
title: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

claim: Prefers weighing the continuum between natural and trained-in scheming, and supplementing with known-actual-scheming or confident non-scheming examples, over relying solely on trained-in behavior, because of disanalogy risks.
quote: Insofar as we had a test bed for directly studying actually scheming that we were reasonably happy with or at least had examples where we were confident scheming wasn't present for some other reason, we could always supplement this test bed with examples of trained-in scheming behavior.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Proposes red-teaming the construction of positive examples with restricted affordances as a possible but unresolved way to make test beds adversarially robust.
quote: Restricting the affordances of red teamers might be viable, but it seems tricky to get a reasonable set of rules.
title: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

claim: Flags open problems: implanting larger interconnected belief systems and non-factual normative beliefs, and whether techniques hold on more capable, situationally aware models.
quote: We focus on isolated factual beliefs, while many AI safety applications may require implanting larger-scale, interconnected belief systems or non-factual, normative beliefs.
title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

claim: Prefers calibrated claims that separate a specific, low-priority failure from the quality of a developer's overall safety execution over sweeping generalizations from one incident.
quote: Therefore, preserving chain-of-thought monitorability was not a top priority for Anthropic, and we don’t take these incidents as representative of Anthropic’s safety execution quality more broadly.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Prefers fixing process weaknesses now, while failures are cheap, over waiting until stakes are existential, and treats repeated incidents as evidence that processes are inadequate.
quote: Anthropic should treat these incidents as evidence that their current development processes aren’t reliable enough for the rate of AI progress they expect, and fix that while the cost of failure is reputational rather than existential.
title: Anthropic repeatedly accidentally trained against the CoT, demonstrating inadequate processes

claim: Interprets weak generalization as possibly a capabilities/sample-efficiency limit or SWE-flavored transfer rather than a clean statement about misalignment, and flags what remains confusing.
quote: So some of the spikiness might just be that the strategies are SWE-flavored and transfer best to SWE-flavored affordances.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Leaves open that longer training, different seeds, or more diverse non-SWE environments could produce coherent reward-seeking or emergent misalignment.
quote: But we can't rule out that a longer or better-tuned run would make the trained models more coherently and consistently reward-seeking.
title: Reward Hacking Without Egregious Misalignment in an RL-Only Setting

claim: Counts absence of verbalized reasoning as weak evidence, but states in advance what clear reasoning would have counted as strong disconfirming evidence.
quote: We do not believe that the absence of reasoning about how the score is used is strong evidence on its own. However, if the reasoning traces had contained clear consideration for downstream consequences, this would have been strong evidence against our claim
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Frames motivation (what drives misbehavior) as the key object of study because motivations predict generalization to other subversion, rather than cataloguing misbehavior instances.
quote: Motivations matter because they help predict generalization: an AI that reward-hacks by rote will generalize differently from one that reward-hacks in pursuit of a goal
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs

claim: Flags that conclusions are limited to leaked-grader agentic coding environments and suggests models may seek apparent success more generally, an open direction.
quote: it’s plausible that tested models care about appearing successful more generally (Greenblatt, 2026), even when this isn’t specified via a grader.
title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs
